analysis.one_liner: Makes all corporate dividends tax-free for individual investors.
analysis.headline: A bill to make stock dividends completely tax-free drew zero cosponsors and died without a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax code so individuals pay no federal income tax on dividends from stocks and mutual funds, starting with tax years ending after enactment. A few payouts would stay taxed as before: capital-gain dividends from mutual funds and real estate trusts, dividends paid through employee stock ownership plans, and dividends from farmer cooperatives. It also keeps tax-free dividends on the books in two places that matter to lower-income families: they would still count as investment income when the IRS checks Earned Income Tax Credit eligibility, and they would still count toward the income that makes Social Security benefits taxable.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of corporate stock and mutual funds. The benefit scales with portfolio size: the wealthiest households, who own most stock and receive most dividend income, would keep the largest share of the tax savings. Investors with taxable brokerage accounts would save something, but money held in 401(k)s and IRAs is already untaxed, so most retirement savers would see no change.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals would pay no federal income tax on dividends they receive, ending the second layer of tax on corporate profits — profits are already taxed at the corporate level before any dividend is paid.
Ordinary dividends paid out by mutual funds would reach fund shareholders tax-free; only capital-gain dividends from funds and real estate investment trusts would stay under the capital-gains rules.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Revenue lost to the dividend exclusion would have to be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or lower spending — costs that land on everyone else and on future taxpayers. States that start their income tax from federal taxable income would also take in less.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state treasuries, all taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts every dividend an individual receives from income tax, and dividend income flows mainly to the households with the largest stock portfolios — so the tax savings would concentrate at the top.

Tax-free dividends would still count as investment income when the IRS decides whether a low-wage family qualifies for the Earned Income Tax Credit, so the families the credit serves get no benefit from the exclusion.
Tax-free dividends would also be added back when calculating whether Social Security benefits are taxable, so some retirees' 'tax-free' dividends could still raise their tax bill.
Workers who own company stock through employee stock ownership plans and patrons of farmer cooperatives are carved out — their dividends would remain fully taxable.
The exclusion takes effect for taxable years ending after enactment, so the revenue loss to the Treasury would be large and immediate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: corporate profits are taxed once at the company and again when paid to shareholders, and ending the second layer would stop penalizing stock ownership. The costs are hard to square with that. Because dividend income flows overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, the savings would go overwhelmingly to the top, while dividends in 401(k)s and IRAs — where most working families hold stock — are already untaxed and gain nothing. The bill taxes ESOP participants and farmer-co-op patrons as before, and it keeps counting tax-free dividends against low-wage families in the EITC and against retirees in the Social Security benefit test. The revenue loss would be large and permanent from the first full year. On balance, this is a well-aimed tax cut for concentrated wealth with a thin story for everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced the same day President Bush proposed ending the dividend tax, it picked up zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in the House tax committee, and expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joe Wilson introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
That referral was the last action ever taken — the bill got no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill would have added a new section to the tax code excluding dividends from individuals' gross income, effective for taxable years ending after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue, and taxpayers broadly avoided the cost. Wealthy shareholders missed a full repeal, though Congress cut the dividend rate to 15% later in 2003 through a separate tax bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; shareholders missed full repeal

for.name: Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 7, 2003 to exclude all individual dividend income from federal tax.

for.name: George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Proposed eliminating individual income taxes on dividends in the economic plan he unveiled in January 2003; this bill was introduced the same day.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee — no hearing, no markup, no vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No member of either party cosponsored the bill and it never came to a vote, so support was never measured beyond its single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Shareholders of publicly traded corporations (concentrated among the wealthiest households)
industries.note: The bill wipes out the individual tax on their dividend income. Because the largest portfolios collect the most dividends, the savings concentrate at the top, financed by the lost federal revenue.

With dividends tax-free to investors, companies could pay dividends more cheaply, which supports share prices and lowers their cost of capital. The gain accrues to owners, while the revenue cost falls on everyone else.

Ordinary fund dividends would become tax-free to fund shareholders, a new selling point for the industry; capital-gain dividends would stay taxed as capital gains. Many middle-class fund investors would share the benefit, though the largest holders gain the most.
